1.pericope_label: LORD, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob. Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people... Turn us, O God of our salvation... Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee? Shew us thy mercy, O LORD, and grant us thy salvation

schools.summary: Ellicott grants that the opening phrase about bringing back might only imply a return to a state of former prosperity in general, but says the context directs us to refer it especially to the return from exile; he gives the verb rendered forgiven its plainer sense, taken away; and he makes the prayer to turn us equivalent to restore us once more, finding in it the motive of the whole song, since if the captivity had taught its lesson the poet wants to know why complete freedom from misfortune did not follow the restoration. Delitzsch supplies a literary genealogy instead of a paraphrase: the second part of the book of Isaiah was written for the Israel of the exile, and it was the incidents of the exile that first unsealed that great and indivisible prophecy, out of which sprang the numerous songs of the psalm collection which recall their common model partly by their allegorising figurative language and partly by their lofty prophetic thoughts of consolation, this Korahite psalm among them. On the petition he denies that the verb forms any bond of connection with the preceding strophe in the sense of restore us again, construing it instead as turn again to us, a prayer that God would manifest himself anew to his people as he did in former days.

Gill takes the land for Canaan, God's inheritance in a peculiar manner, and the people for those he chose above all others, brought out of Egyptian bondage and led through the wilderness. He reads the forgiveness through the atonement: the iniquity was taken from them and laid on Christ, who bore it and took it away so that it shall never return to their destruction, and the wrath was gathered up and poured out on the surety, so that nothing of the kind shall fall on them here or hereafter. The prayer to turn us he takes for converting grace, either at first conversion or after backslidings, and perhaps for the conversion of the Jews in the latter day, when the Lord will turn them to himself and turn away iniquity from them; and he distinguishes carefully on the question of anger, since God is angry with the wicked every day and for ever, their life being a continued series of sin without repentance, while his anger with his own people endures but a moment. Calvin sets out the psalm as a threefold argument: God having afflicted his people with new troubles and calamities after their return from captivity in Babylon, they first make mention of their deliverance as a reason why he should not leave unfinished the work of his grace, then complain of the long continuance of their afflictions, and third, inspired with hope and confidence, triumph in the blessedness promised them, since their restoration to their own country was connected with the kingdom of Christ, from which they anticipated an abundance of all good things.

Clarke dates the psalm during or even after the return from the Babylonish captivity and divides it in four, thanksgiving for restoration to the divine favour, prayer for further mercies, the psalmist waiting for a gracious answer, and the assurance of blessing received with exultation. On the forgiveness he renders the verb thou hast borne, or carried away, the iniquity, an allusion to the ceremony of the scapegoat, and takes the covering to mean that the offensiveness and abominable nature of the sin no longer appear, the whole being put out of sight; on the pause that follows he writes simply that this is true, and that their return to their own land is the full proof. He carries the same metaphor into the next verse, where the wrath is gathered up and carried away along with the iniquities. His prayer is for a completed restoration, since the Israelites were not restored all at once: a few returned with Zerubbabel and some more with Ezra and Nehemiah, while a great number remained in Babylonia, Media, Assyria, Egypt and other parts. Wesley glosses briefly and locally: the captivity means the captives, turn us means restore us to our former tranquillity and free us from the troubles we yet groan under, and the reviving is a second reviving in bringing home the rest of our brethren and restraining our enemies.

Henry notices who is speaking before he notices what is said: the church, in affliction and distress, is here by direction from God making her application to God, so ready is God to hear and answer the prayers of his people that by his Spirit in the word and in the heart he indites their petitions and puts words into their mouths. They are to acknowledge with thankfulness the great things God had done for them and their fathers, since the sense of present afflictions should not drown the remembrance of former mercies. Spurgeon attends to the name invoked: the self-existent, all-sufficient Jehovah is addressed by the name he revealed to Moses when his people were in bondage, and it is wise to dwell upon that view of the divine character which arouses the sweetest memories of his love, though sweeter still is the dear name of Our Father with which Christians have learned to begin their prayers. Canaan is called the Lord's land because he chose it for his people, conveyed it by covenant, conquered it by his power and dwelt in it in mercy. On the questions of the fifth verse he turns the interrogatives into pleading: we are in time as yet and not in eternity, and does not time come to an end, and therefore the wrath with it? Shall sons suffer for their fathers' faults, and punishment become an entailed inheritance? Every word is an argument, for men in distress never waste words.

Augustine reads the psalm through its title. Understanding no other end than that of which the Apostle speaks, since Christ is the end of the law, he says that in placing the words for the end at the head of the title the psalmist directed our heart to Christ; and if we fix our gaze on him we shall not stray, for he is himself the Truth unto which we are eager to arrive and himself the Way by which we run. He then accounts for the tenses that puzzle the historical readers: the prophet sings to him of the future and uses words as it were of past time, speaking of things future as if they were already done, because with God that which is future has already happened.

debates.question: What does the prayer turn us ask for?

positions.view: Restoration to their former tranquillity and freedom from the troubles they still groan under.
Restore us once more; the puzzle of why the restoration brought no complete freedom is the motive of the whole song.
Not restore us again at all, but turn again to us: a prayer that God manifest himself anew as in former days.
A completed restoration of all the dispersed, since the people came back only in instalments.
Converting grace, and perhaps the conversion of the Jews in the latter day.

debates.question: Is the psalm read of its own history or of Christ?

positions.view: Of Christ from the title onward, since for the end means that Christ is the end of the law.
Of the restoration, but a restoration connected with the kingdom of Christ.
Of the atonement: the iniquity taken from the people and laid on Christ, who bore it away.
Of the historical return from Babylon.

debates.question: What is the reviving asked for in the sixth verse?

positions.view: A nation becoming once more numerous, pious and powerful.
A second reviving: the rest of the brethren brought home and the enemies restrained.
Conversion, which is a resurrection, men dead in trespasses being quickened by the Spirit.

outliers.note: Reads the whole psalm from its superscription and explains its past tenses by God's eternity, where what is future has already happened.
Derives the psalm's figurative language and thoughts of consolation from the second part of Isaiah, treating it as one of a family of exile-era songs.

themes: Lord, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob.
Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people, thou hast covered all their sin. Selah.
Thou hast taken away all thy wrath: thou hast turned thyself from the fierceness of thine anger.
Turn us, O God of our salvation, and cause thine anger toward us to cease.
Wilt thou be angry with us for ever? wilt thou draw out thine anger to all generations?
Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?
Shew us thy mercy, O Lord, and grant us thy salvation.

8.pericope_label: I will hear what God the LORD will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people... Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other. Truth shall spring out of the earth... Righteousness shall go before him; and shall set us in the way of his steps

schools.summary: Ellicott says the word peace comprehends all that the nation sighed for, and that to Christians it has a higher meaning still, which directed the choice of this psalm for Christmas Day, while the folly warned against most probably implies idolatry. On the meeting of the attributes he confirms the picture from the verb itself, which is used of those who should be friends but whom circumstances have sundered. He grounds the springing of truth in the harvest: faithfulness is depicted as springing out of the earth because the renewal of fertility has re-established the conviction of God's faithfulness towards his people, which had been shaken, while the righteousness in parallel with it, hidden like the sun behind a cloud, is now seen showing its benign face once more in the skies, the verb being one used of bending forward as from a window or battlement. He would render the last verse righteousness shall walk in front of him and follow in his steps, and observes that nothing is more instructive than the blending of material and moral blessings in the closing verses, which do go together, as experience, especially national experience, testifies. Delitzsch pursues the picture of the future: after God's faithfulness to the promises has descended like dew, faithfulness to the covenant springs up out of the land as the fruit of that fertilising influence, and gracious justice looks down from heaven, smiling favour and dispensing blessing, so that God gives everything that is only and always good and the land answers with its increase.

Gill has the psalmist speak in the name of the people of the Jews, refusing to be still and quiet but waiting and listening for an answer from the Lord, who speaks by his providences, his word and his Spirit. He describes those to whom the salvation is nigh as having a true sense of sin and folly, humbled for it and departing from it, with a reverential affection for God and a sense of his pardoning mercy; and he distinguishes the temporal salvation, which is a present help in time of trouble, from the spiritual and eternal, which was then near being accomplished by Christ. On the meeting of the attributes he has grace and truth meet in Christ, since mercy is the original of salvation and it was pity for the lost human race which moved God to send him. On the springing of truth he offers three readings and prefers the last: the gospel, the word of truth, which sprang up at once in the land of Judea as if it came out of the earth and thence went into the Gentile world; or the truth of grace which God desires in the inward parts, springing up in hearts made like cultivated ground by the Spirit; or rather Christ himself, who is the way, the truth and the life, and who, though he is the Lord from heaven, may be said with respect to his incarnation to spring out of the earth. On the last verse he takes righteousness for a righteous person, following a rabbi, and suggests John the Baptist, the forerunner and harbinger who prepared the way.

Clarke has the psalmist go as a prophet to consult the Lord, wait an answer from the spirit of prophecy, and then relate it to the people, adding that the peace promised is prosperity to the people in general and to his saints in particular, and that the warning is against abusing the mercy of God by sinning any more against him. On the glory he wants the worship restored, the temple rebuilt and the divine symbol of God's presence back in its place, since the pure and undefiled religion of God preached and experienced in a nation is the glory of that land, and the second temple, far inferior as a building to Solomon's, had the superior glory of being visited by Jesus Christ. His treatment of the four attributes is the fullest in the chapter: he would render the verse mercy and truth have met on the way, righteousness and peace have embraced, and finds in it a beauty he thinks unnoticed, that mercy and peace stand on one side and truth and righteousness on the other, since truth requires righteousness and mercy calls for peace; they meet on the way, one going to make inquisition for sin and the other to plead for reconciliation, and having adjusted their differences and blended their claims in one common interest, peace and righteousness immediately embrace. He takes the good thing of the twelfth verse for the supreme good, the summum bonum for which man has searched in vain through all his generations. Wesley narrows the saints to those who are truly God's people rather than all who are called so, dates the salvation as nigh because the seventy weeks determined in the vision were begun, notes that not only Christian but even Jewish writers understand the place of the redemption by the Messiah, and spreads the four attributes across that work, God's mercy in redeeming Israel and converting the Gentiles, his truth in fulfilling the promise, his righteousness in punishing sin on his Son and conferring righteousness on guilty creatures, and his peace with sinners.

Henry hears in the eighth verse an answer of peace, and has the psalmist stand upon his watch-tower to hear what God will say, as a prophet did. The resolution intimates the stilling of his passions, his grief and his fear and the tumult of his spirit: compose thyself, O my soul, in a humble silence to attend upon God and wait his motions, for I have spoken enough, or too much, and now I will hear what God will speak and welcome his holy will. It intimates also the raising of his expectation, since now that he has been at prayer he looks for something very great and very kind; and Henry draws the practical rule, that if we would have God hear what we say to him by prayer, we must be ready to hear what he says to us by his word. Spurgeon has the sacred poet, having offered earnest intercession for the afflicted but penitent nation, await a response from the sacred oracle in the true spirit of faith, pausing in joyful confidence and then giving utterance to his hopes in the richest form of song. When we believe that God hears us, he says, it is but natural that we should be eager to hear him, for only from him can come the word which speaks peace to troubled spirits, the voices of men being a plaister far too narrow for the sore, while God's voice is power: he speaks and it is done.

debates.question: What is the folly they are warned not to return to?

positions.view: Most probably idolatry.
Abusing the mercy of their God by sinning any more against him.

debates.question: What is the truth that springs out of the earth?

positions.view: Faithfulness to the covenant, springing up as the fruit of God's own faithfulness after it has descended like dew.
Faithfulness, since renewed fertility re-established a conviction of God's faithfulness that had been shaken.
True religion, diffused over the world by the preaching of Christ and his apostles.
The gospel, or the grace of faith in the heart, or rather Christ himself, springing from the earth by his incarnation.

debates.question: What is the righteousness that goes before him?

positions.view: A righteous person, following a rabbi: probably John the Baptist, the forerunner.
A harbinger who fulfils all righteousness and makes us walk in the ways wherein he walks.
Righteousness walking in front of him and following in his steps, blending material with moral blessing.

outliers.note: Stages the four attributes as two parties on a road, one going to make inquisition for sin and the other to plead for reconciliation, who settle their claims before embracing.
Notes the psalm's liturgical use on Christmas Day and closes his comment with an English ode addressed to Duty.

themes: I will hear what God the Lord will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people, and to his saints: but let them not turn again to folly.
Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land.
Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven.
Yea, the Lord shall give that which is good; and our land shall yield her increase.
Righteousness shall go before him; and shall set us in the way of his steps.
